title: How Grow Houses Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how indoor marijuana grow houses operate, based on a How Stuff Works article by Robert Lamb. They open with news of California's Proposition 19 and marijuana-use statistics, then cover hydroponics, high-wattage grow lights, heat and CO2 control, electricity theft and generators, water-meter tampering, staffing with exploited immigrant workers, concealment from neighbors and police, and the neighborhood harms (fire risk, pollution, mold, property values). The episode ends with a listener mail about voodoo and the hosts' promotional updates (Facebook, Twitter, Kiva).

segments.title: Opening banter and Prop 19 lead-in
segments.summary: Hosts welcome listeners, mention a Guatemala text donation campaign for Co-ed, and discuss California's Proposition 19 on marijuana legalization and its outdoor-only growing allowance, leading into the topic of grow houses.

segments.title: Marijuana use statistics
segments.summary: Worldwide and US marijuana use figures from a UN report are discussed, including countries with high per-capita use and US survey numbers, plus Atlanta arrest statistics.

segments.title: What a grow house is and its risks
segments.summary: A grow house is a home dedicated to growing marijuana as a business. Operators face robbery, police, and pressure from buyers, and the plant's cultivation is a sophisticated farming operation aimed at potent buds.

segments.title: Hydroponics and growing methods
segments.summary: Growers can use soil or hydroponics, which grows plants in nutrient-rich water without soil. Indoor growers can produce pot with much higher THC than outdoor pot.

segments.title: Grow lights, light cycles, and heat
segments.summary: Grow houses are sealed off and use high-wattage horticultural bulbs, around 1000 watts each, to mimic the sun. Growers shorten the light cycle to trigger flowering, only female plants are kept, and the heat can reach about 100 degrees Fahrenheit, requiring air conditioning and fans.

segments.title: Electricity theft and electrical hazards
segments.summary: Grow houses draw far more power than a typical house can handle, so operators may rewire the house or tap the grid with help from power company insiders. This is dangerous to neighbors and the operator. Generators are an alternative but are loud, costly, and prone to failure. Power bills are another giveaway.

segments.title: Water theft and CO2 and pest control
segments.summary: Growers use large amounts of water, and some drill holes in water meter paddles to avoid detection. CO2 levels are raised with burners and charcoal filtration is used to control smell and insects by suffocating pests.

segments.title: Staffing, investors, and exploited workers
segments.summary: Grow houses are often funded by secret investors who never visit. Workers may be illegal immigrants indentured to repay smuggling debts, and some are exploited, including forced prostitution in California, with the hosts comparing the situations.

segments.title: Concealment and neighborhood impacts
segments.summary: Grow houses are kept in suburbs and blend in with normal homes, avoiding infrared detection by using a room within a room. Neighbors face robbery risk, electrical hazards, pollution, a 2008 Humboldt County diesel spill, toxic mold, insurance increases, and lower property values. Grow houses cluster in foreclosed neighborhoods in South Florida, and busts include a 2,000-plant Lake County, Florida house and a Tennessee tunnel.

segments.title: Closing discussion on drug coverage and the article
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difficulty of covering drug topics without sounding like a tutorial, reiterate that the show does not endorse illegal activity, and point listeners to Robert Lamb's article.

segments.title: Listener mail: voodoo story
segments.summary: A listener from Tri-Cities, Washington shares a story about dating a man who practiced voodoo as a bocor, with statues in his home, and his Catholic roommate.

segments.title: Sign-off and promotions
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, invite emails, and promote the Facebook page, Twitter following, blog, and the Kiva lending team.
